label: lf-fire-regs
topic: How a new bio-based fire-retardant coating or material is tested against fire regulations (EU, UK, US, intumescent practice), evidence that finding testers is a bottleneck, and bio-based flame-retardant chemistry numbers
summary: Fetch date for every item below is 2026-11-13. Many publisher pages (iso.org, astm.org, ANSI/BSI previews) returned HTTP 403, so for ISO/ASTM/EN standards the paywalled text and in several cases the edition status could NOT be confirmed from a fetched page. What was read: the Euroclass table (EN 13501-1 Table 1, via legislation.gov.uk copy of Reg 2016/364), UK gov.uk Approved Document B page, ICC 2027 cycle notice, Genorma/DIN/EVS catalogue pages for EN 16623, EN 13381-8 and ISO 5660-1, Intertek E84 page, a UL 94 explainer, and several open-access papers. Pass criteria in numbers were obtained for Euroclasses A1-E, ASTM E84 classes, UL 94 V ratings. Not obtained: numeric pass criteria and sample counts for ISO 1182 beyond the Euroclass table, ISO 1716 sample count, EN 13823 specimen count, NFPA 285 numeric limits, ASTM E119 end-point numbers, E2768 criteria, EN 13381-8 specimen count, ISO 5660 sample size. Bottleneck evidence is real but qualitative: UKAS-accredited capacity shortage stated by Warringtonfire (2024), long waiting times stated by a Danish lab (CFPA-E), a USD 0.5-1M cost for one full-scale mass-timber apartment fire test program (ENR 2017). No count of accredited fire labs for any region, no queue times in weeks and no per-test price were found. Bio-based chemistry: phytic-acid layer-by-layer coatings on cotton raise LOI from 18% to 26-31% and cut pHRR by ~57-63%; mycelium composites peak near 180-200 kW/m2 at 50 kW/m2 flux versus roughly 200 for the substrate; phytic-acid treated wood LOI 31.8-37.2% (as quoted in a review). Most lab-scale numbers are LOI, cone or MCC on textile or foam, which are NOT the tests the building regulations use (SBI, E84, E119), a key gap for any Lean/Delphi elimination-certificate idea.
lay_summary: Before a new building material can be sold, it has to be burned in a standard test and given a grade. In Europe the grade is a letter from A1 down to F, and in the US the tests have names like ASTM E84 and E119. The tests are done only by approved laboratories, and I found a lab company saying there is not enough approved capacity in the UK, and a Danish lab saying testers face long waiting times. One big US wood fire test program cost half a million to a million dollars. Plant-based flame retardants such as phytic acid and chitosan look good in small lab tests, but those small tests are not the ones the building rules use, so a computer-side filter could save test slots only if it predicts the official test results. I could not find published counts of labs, queue times in weeks, or price lists.

findings.claim: EN 13501-1 Euroclass A1 requires EN ISO 1182 (furnace) and EN ISO 1716 (bomb calorimeter) with temperature rise <= 30 C, mass loss <= 50%, no sustained flaming, and gross calorific potential <= 2.0 MJ/kg for main components.
findings.value: dT<=30 C; mass loss<=50%; tf=0 s; PCS<=2.0 MJ/kg (A1); A2: dT<=50 C, tf<=20 s, PCS<=3.0 MJ/kg
findings.source: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/364/data.htm (Table 1 as reproduced; fetched 2026-11-13). This is the 2016 Commission Delegated Regulation text, not the EN 13501-1:2018 standard itself, so the edition of the standard behind the numbers is not confirmed.

findings.claim: Euroclass B requires the SBI (EN 13823) FIGRA <= 120 W/s, THR600s <= 7.5 MJ and lateral flame spread short of the specimen edge, plus EN ISO 11925-2 with 30 s exposure and Fs <= 150 mm within 60 s. Class C: FIGRA <= 250 W/s, THR600s <= 15 MJ. Class D: FIGRA <= 750 W/s. Class E: small-flame test only, Fs <= 150 mm within 20 s (15 s exposure).
findings.evidence_quote: B: FIGRA ≤ 120 Ws– 1; and LFS < edge of specimen; and THR600s ≤ 7,5 MJ

findings.claim: ASTM E84 grades materials by Flame Spread Index: Class A 0-25, Class B 26-75, Class C 76-200, each with Smoke Developed Index up to 450; the standard specimen is 24 in wide by 24 ft long and the test runs 10 minutes.
findings.value: FSI A 0-25, B 26-75, C 76-200; SDI max 450; 24 in x 24 ft; 10 min
findings.source: https://intertek.com/building/standards/astm-e84 (fetched 2026-11-13). astm.org page returned 403, so edition (believed E84-25 from memory, UNVERIFIED) not confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: The standard test specimen size is 24 inches wide by 24 feet long.

findings.claim: UL 94 vertical burn V-0 requires afterflame <= 10 s per specimen after each flame application, <= 50 s total for five specimens, afterglow <= 30 s, and no cotton ignition by drips; V-1 allows <= 30 s each and <= 250 s total; V-2 allows cotton ignition.
findings.value: V-0: 10 s / 50 s total / 30 s afterglow; V-1,V-2: 30 s / 250 s / 60 s; five specimens
findings.source: https://mgchemicals.com/knowledgebase/white-papers/understanding-the-ul94-vertical-burn-test/ (fetched 2026-11-13); secondary explainer, not the UL standard text, edition not stated.

findings.claim: ISO 5660-1:2015 (corrected version 2021-01) specifies the cone calorimeter method; Amendment 1:2019 (valid from 2019-08-06) is the newest item and amends rather than replaces it. No replacement edition was seen in the catalogue page.
findings.evidence_quote: ISO 5660-1:2015 specifies a method for assessing the heat release rate and dynamic smoke production rate of specimens

findings.claim: EN 16623:2015 (reactive coatings for steel) is published, in 'periodical review' stage 90.20 dated 2026-07-15, and itself relies on CEN fire resistance test methods (EN 13381-6, EN 13381-8, prEN 13381-9) without setting performance levels.
findings.evidence_quote: It relies on CEN fire resistance test methods (EN 13381-6, EN 13381-8, and prEN 13381-9) and does not specify required performance levels

findings.claim: EN 13381-8:2013 (DIN edition 2013-08, marked CURRENT) is the test method for reactive fire protection applied to steel beams and columns; no draft or newer version noted on the page. Specimen count not found.
findings.evidence_quote: This European Standard specifies a test method for determining the contribution made by applied reactive fire protection

findings.claim: UK Approved Document B (England) is the 2019 edition incorporating 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments, with 2026 and 2029 amendments published but not yet collated; 2024-update note says national classes (BS 476 fire tests) are being withdrawn with a transition period.
findings.evidence_quote: withdraw national classes (BS 476 fire tests). Transition periods for both policy updates will offer certainty to investors.

findings.claim: ICC reports final results of the 2024-2026 code development cycle (Group A and B) posted 2026-07-22, with the codes to be published later in 2026; the cycle after the 2024 IBC feeds the 2027 IBC. Chapter 7/ASTM E119 outcomes were not read.
findings.evidence_quote: will be published and available in both print and digital formats later this year

findings.claim: The 2023 NFPA 285 edition added Annex B (extensions of results); the 2024 IBC added routes to show compliance (direct testing, listed assemblies, approved analysis). Next NFPA 285 edition not found.
findings.value: NFPA 285-2023 (Annex B added); IBC 2024 s1402.8 three routes
findings.evidence_quote: the 2023 edition of NFPA 285 introduced Annex B

findings.claim: A UK fire-test provider says manufacturers face a shortage of UKAS-accredited testing capacity; it added slots on three furnaces and is building a GBP 23m facility (80% size increase), due early 2025 (article dated 2024-02-23). No lead times in weeks were given.
findings.evidence_quote: manufacturers are facing a lack of UKAS-accredited testing capacity today.

findings.claim: A European fire association notice says that before a new Nordic detection-systems lab, manufacturers faced capacity shortages and long waiting times; Europe lacks facilities for detection-system testing. No durations or lab counts. (Fire detection, not coatings.)
findings.evidence_quote: Europe lacks facilities for testing fire detection systems.

findings.claim: One full-scale US mass-timber furnished-apartment fire test program was estimated at USD 500,000 to 1 million, mostly paid by the American Wood Council (article 2017-08-16).
findings.evidence_quote: the cost will be about $500,000 to $1 million.

findings.claim: Some European fire labs are accredited to ISO/IEC 17025 only and some Notified Bodies only to ISO/IEC 17065; many labs hold both. So 'accredited lab' and 'notified body' are separate counts and no total was published on that page.
findings.evidence_quote: there are fire laboratories only EN ISO/IEC 17025 accredited and Notified Bodies only EN ISO/IEC 17065 accredited.

findings.claim: Phytic acid-based layer-by-layer coating on cotton: untreated LOI 18-19%; 8 bilayers LOI 26%, 15 bilayers 31%; pHRR reduction 57.0% (8 BL) to 63.3% (15 BL), average ~61%; 10+ bilayers pass vertical flame test with 0 s afterflame; add-on 12.4-20.1%.
findings.value: LOI 18->26-31%; pHRR -57 to -63% (microscale calorimetry per search summary); add-on 12-20%
findings.evidence_quote: applying 10 or more bilayers renders cotton self-extinguishing and able to pass the vertical flame test.

findings.claim: Phytic acid / polyvinylamine LbL coating on cotton: MCC pHRR 216 W/g uncoated vs 42.8 W/g at 15 bilayers; THR 10.7 vs 4.2 kJ/g; TGA residue at 700 C under N2 8.7% vs 29.1%; 15 BL add-on 18.8% (2.0% P, 1.4% N); afterflame 64 s burn-down vs 0 s. LOI and time to ignition not reported.
findings.evidence_quote: uncoated fabric burned completely down within 64 s, while 10 and 15 BL showed 0 s

findings.claim: Mycelium-wheat grain composites in the cone calorimeter at 50 kW/m2: peak heat release about 200 kW/m2 for the 0-day control and about 180 kW/m2 for 6-18 day composites; TGA residue ~23 wt% at 600 C vs 19 wt% for grain. Time to ignition measured but not tabulated in text.
findings.evidence_quote: approximately 23 wt% remaining at 600 °C compared to 19 wt% for wheat grains at the same temperature.

findings.claim: Review of biomass wood flame retardants quotes phytic-acid-based treatments giving wood LOI of 37.2% (cellulose lumen treatment) and 31.8% (phytic acid + uracil). The page text gave no pHRR/THR/char numbers for chitosan or lignin; tannin not covered in the part read.
findings.value: LOI 37.2% and 31.8% (as quoted from cited primary papers)
findings.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9966695/ ; DOI 10.3390/polym15040950 (Liang et al. 2023; fetched 2026-11-13, first 100000 of 132416 characters read)
findings.evidence_quote: FR wood can achieve a 31.8% limit oxygen index value

findings.claim: Search-result snippets (NOT fetched pages; confidence low): chitosan-phytic acid Schiff-base cotton LOI 17.6% -> 30.6% with pHRR ~-80% and THR ~-60%; alginate/mica coating on polyurethane foam LOI 16% -> 30.5% with UL 94 V-0; lignin-containing systems: V-0 and LOI 31.95% in PLA vs ~19-21% neat, kraft lignin char up to 40%; bio-derived intumescent on polyamide textile LOI 23.5% -> 27%, pHRR -56%.
findings.source: WebSearch result summaries 2026-11-13 pointing to https://bohrium.dp.tech/paper/arxiv/671f3d3801d2a3fbfca8d95d ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39706424/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12251784 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6515164/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13673877 (the last two PMC fetches hit a browser-check page and were not read)
findings.evidence_quote: The limiting oxygen index was increased from 23.5% to 27%, and the peak heat release rate measured by cone calorimetry was reduced by 56%.

key_claims.claim: Regulatory reaction-to-fire grades are set by large-scale or standardised tests (SBI FIGRA/THR600s, E84 flame-spread index, UL 94 burn times), not by the LOI / cone / MCC numbers that bio-based chemistry papers report, so lab-scale gains cannot be assumed to translate into a grade.
key_claims.value: e.g. Euroclass B needs FIGRA<=120 W/s and THR600s<=7.5 MJ; papers report LOI and pHRR
key_claims.evidence_quote: B: FIGRA ≤ 120 Ws– 1; and LFS < edge of specimen; and THR600s ≤ 7,5 MJ

key_claims.claim: Testing capacity is described as a constraint by labs themselves (UK UKAS capacity shortage; Nordic long waiting times), and full-scale programs can cost USD 0.5-1M, but no published queue times in weeks, per-test prices or lab counts were found.
key_claims.value: GBP 23m new UK facility; USD 0.5-1M program
key_claims.evidence_quote: manufacturers are facing a lack of UKAS-accredited testing capacity today.

key_claims.claim: Phytic-acid layer-by-layer coatings are the best-documented bio-based flame retardant here: cotton LOI 18% -> 31% and pHRR -63% at 15 bilayers, self-extinguishing at 10+ bilayers.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Cotton treated with 8 BL has an LOI of 26%, which increases to 31% with 15 BL.

recommendations: Use the standardised grading numbers only as targets: Euroclass B (FIGRA<=120 W/s, THR600s<=7.5 MJ), E84 Class A (FSI<=25), UL 94 V-0 (<=10 s). Any Lean elimination rule must be expressed in those units, not LOI.
Before building, obtain the paid standards or lab-supplied test protocols for EN 13823, ISO 1182, ASTM E119 and NFPA 285 to get specimen counts and end-point numbers, which this round could not read.
Get quotes (not contact with individuals, per brief rules) from accredited lab price lists such as RISE or UKAS-listed labs to fill cost and lead-time gaps; this round found none.

Treat Delphi as a screen on small-scale proxies (cone calorimeter pHRR, time to ignition, char yield) calibrated against the few papers that report both cone data and a regulatory class; none were found here.
Re-check ISO and ASTM edition status via the ISO and ASTM catalogues from a browser, since fetch returned 403 for both.

glossary.plain: The lowest oxygen percentage in the air at which a material keeps burning; air has about 21%, so higher LOI is safer.
The highest rate at which a burning sample gives off heat; lower is better.
A bench-top test that heats a small square of material under a cone-shaped heater and measures the heat it gives off.
A medium-scale European test where a corner of two wall panels is set alight by a gas burner; its results decide Euroclasses B to D.
A fire growth speed number from the SBI test, in watts per second; lower is better.
Total heat released during the first 600 seconds of the SBI test.
A paint that swells into a thick insulating char when hot, protecting what is under it, such as steel.
How much of the material is left as charred residue after heating; more char usually means better fire protection.
The UK accreditation body, and the international rule set a test laboratory must meet to be an officially approved tester.
A milligram-scale lab test of heat release; cheaper but not what building rules use.
